core_concepts: It’s good to be a seeker
When I was in the second grade, I noticed a thin book on my dad’s office table
“Dad, what’s that book about?” I asked
“Why don’t you read it and tell me what you think it’s about?”
That answer was pretty typical of my dad
The book tells the story of a seagull who wants to fly faster than any other gull ever believed was possible
Jonathan Livingston Seagull influenced my worldview more than any other book I read growing up
If you take away one thing from this book, I hope you realize that, in different ways, all of us unwittingly let our own self-imposed limits govern how we think and act throughout our lives

mechanisms_or_explanations: —RICHARD BACH, J L S When I was in the second grade, I noticed a thin book on my dad’s office table
And so much more.) When I summarized it to my dad, I don’t remember the exact words I used
If you take away one thing from this book, I hope you realize that, in different ways, all of us unwittingly let our own self-imposed limits govern how we think and act throughout our lives
The trickiest part is that they can be so embedded in our assumptions we fail to even realize they exist, not to mention how they hold us back
The same limits are true when it comes to how we think about start-ups
With start-ups, the first types of self-imposed limits come from how we think
We create imaginary experiences of the future when we make believe that a cardboard box is a rocket ship
We don’t worry about being “wrong” when we try things
We observe that rewards come from learning how to answer questions that have already been answered
Having the “right answers” leads to good grades, a prestigious degree, or a job that pays well
We also learn to define objectives in our personal lives, like how much exercise we get or how much we should save for retirement
In my specialty of start-ups, I’ve noticed that many people miss how this mindset limits finding breakthroughs
critical_qualifiers: But sooner or later you have to be a finder, and then it is good to give what you have found, a gift into the world for whoever will accept it
But the idea I’d taken from it was that the biggest limits in the world are the limits of your mind, your imagination, and your actions—not the limits of the world itself
The trickiest part is that they can be so embedded in our assumptions we fail to even realize they exist, not to mention how they hold us back
And by recognizing those limits, you can free yourself from them, which makes it far more likely you will become a pattern breaker and create a breakthrough that honors the gift of your time
But as we grow up, life starts to teach us to think in ways that will limit our ability to conceive of breakthroughs
All these ways of thinking help us succeed but rarely lead to pattern-breaking discoveries
First, we often fall into conventional thinking when coming up with start-up ideas

But thinking in this conventional way limits us because it usually has an embedded but limiting assumption: that the future will be a new and improved continuation of the present, defined by rules already set by others
Can we develop an insight into the future that harnesses these inflections in a nonobvious way?
Are we at the frontier of powerful technology, seeing firsthand how it can change our lives and the lives of others?
